subsystems.name: Senolytic payload
subsystems.role: the active molecule that pushes a senescent cell into programmed cell death.
parts: flavonoids such as quercetin and fisetin

subsystems.name: Selectivity mechanism
subsystems.role: makes the drug kill senescent cells while leaving healthy ones alone.
parts: identification of the survival pathways senescent cells depend on
sparing of the same targets in normal tissue

subsystems.name: Formulation and dosing
subsystems.role: gets the drug to the right tissue in short, intermittent pulses.

subsystems.name: Biomarkers and patient selection
subsystems.role: finds who has enough senescent cells to benefit, and proves the drug worked.
parts: blood panels of senescence-associated secretory factors

subsystems.name: Safety management
subsystems.role: contains side effects from hitting targets that healthy cells also use.

subsystems.name: Clinical trial and regulatory package
subsystems.role: turns a mechanism into an approved medicine.

buildSteps.title: Pick a survival pathway
buildSteps.detail: Researchers identify the anti-apoptotic proteins that senescent cells rely on but normal cells can partly do without.

buildSteps.title: Screen candidate compounds
buildSteps.detail: Existing drugs and natural compounds are tested for the ability to kill senescent cells in culture while sparing dividing cells.

buildSteps.title: Optimise selectivity
buildSteps.detail: Molecules are chemically modified to improve potency, tissue distribution and how quickly they clear from the body.

buildSteps.title: Formulate for delivery
buildSteps.detail: The compound is made into a tablet, carrier or injectable, and a dosing schedule is designed.

buildSteps.title: Test in aged animals
buildSteps.detail: Rodent models of ageing or specific disease are treated, then tissue and blood are checked for reduced senescent burden and improved function.

buildSteps.title: Establish human safety
buildSteps.detail: Early-phase trials give the drug to small groups, first at single rising doses, to find a tolerable range.

buildSteps.title: Choose a disease and measure benefit
buildSteps.detail: Later trials target one condition, such as lung fibrosis or a joint disease, against a control group.

buildSteps.title: Validate the biomarker
buildSteps.detail: Tissue and blood markers are compared before and after treatment, so the mechanism is confirmed, not just a symptom change.

buildSteps.title: Seek approval
buildSteps.detail: If benefit outweighs harm in that disease, regulators can approve the drug for it — and long-term follow-up begins.

prerequisites.why: without a way to measure senescent burden in living people, dosing and patient selection stay guesswork.

prerequisites.tech: Compounds that hit BCL-2 family survival proteins
prerequisites.why: inhibitors exist and are used in cancer, but they also affect platelets and immune cells, which need those proteins.

prerequisites.tech: Drugs with human safety data in older adults
prerequisites.why: repositioning existing medicines shortens the path compared with inventing a molecule from scratch.

prerequisites.tech: Accepted clinical endpoints for age-related disease
prerequisites.why: regulators approve treatments for a named disease, not for ageing itself, so trials must be aimed at specific conditions.

prerequisites.tech: Manufacturing and quality control for small molecules
prerequisites.why: standard pharmaceutical production already covers most candidate senolytics.

pathway.milestone: early-phase trials of senolytic combinations in fibrosis, joint disease and kidney disease
pathway.unlocks: first human safety and dosing data.

pathway.milestone: validated blood or tissue tests that show senescent burden falling after treatment
pathway.unlocks: selection of patients most likely to respond.

pathway.milestone: mid- and late-stage trials showing clinical benefit in one named disease
safer, more selective molecules and intermittent preventive regimens
pathway.unlocks: possible use before disease appears, if long-term safety is proven.
